triage.name: Esophageal atresia
triage.reason: Newborn with excessive secretions, choking and cyanosis with feeds; diagnosed by failure to pass a feeding tube and imaging, often with a tracheoesophageal fistula.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'chest and abdominal x-ray (babygram)' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']

age.peak: newborn (first hours to days of life)

demographics: Occurs in about 1 in 2,500 to 4,500 live births
Most cases are diagnosed in the newborn period
comorbidities: VACTERL association (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb anomalies)
family_history: Most cases are sporadic; a small minority have an affected sibling or a parent with a tracheoesophageal anomaly

chief_complaints.text: My baby is drooling and spitting up a lot
My baby chokes and turns blue when we try to feed
My baby is having trouble breathing

hpi.onset: Within the first hours to days of life; often noted immediately after birth or at the first feeding
hpi.progression: Persistent and worsening with each attempted feed; respiratory distress may develop if not recognized
hpi.quality: Frothy secretions, coughing, gagging and choking during feeds
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can be life-threatening if feeds are continued
hpi.timing: Continuous drooling; choking and cyanosis occur with feeding attempts

associated_symptoms.text: Frothy white bubbles coming from the mouth
Turning blue around the lips or face with feeds

pertinent_negatives: Normal feeding without any coughing or choking
Passage of a normal feeding tube into the stomach

negatives: Weight loss after birth beyond normal

argues_against: Primary respiratory infection without feeding-related symptoms
Isolated gastrointestinal obstruction without respiratory symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: Premature or small-for-gestational-age infants may have milder or delayed symptoms, and the diagnosis may be suspected only when a feeding tube cannot be passed or when respiratory distress develops.
missing_classic_features: Dramatic choking and cyanosis with first feed

atypical.how_it_differs: Rarely, a mild or missed case presents later in childhood with recurrent aspiration, coughing with feeds, or failure to thrive; this is more typical of an isolated tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia.
missing_classic_features: Inability to pass a feeding tube

general.mild: Newborn in no distress at rest, but with continuous frothy oral secretions; may be small for gestational age or premature
general.moderate: Newborn with copious oral secretions, coughing, gagging and mild respiratory distress; becomes cyanotic with feeding attempts
general.severe: Ill-appearing newborn with respiratory distress, grunting, retractions and cyanosis during feeds; unable to handle secretions
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, cyanotic, apneic or gasping newborn with severe respiratory distress; requires immediate airway management

findings.maneuver: Inspect the mouth and oropharynx and observe for pooling secretions
findings.finding: Copious frothy white secretions pooling in the mouth and pharynx, requiring frequent suctioning

findings.maneuver: Attempt to pass a soft feeding tube through the mouth or nose into the stomach
findings.finding: The tube meets resistance and coils in the upper esophagus or pharynx; it cannot be advanced into the stomach

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant during an attempted feed or while handling secretions
findings.finding: Perioral or generalized cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with suctioning

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant during an attempted feed
findings.finding: Choking, gagging and coughing with the first swallows of milk

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant at rest and during feeding for work of breathing
findings.finding: Tachypnea, nasal flaring, intercostal or subcostal retractions and grunting
Crackles or coarse breath sounds from aspirated secretions
A distended, tympanitic abdomen suggesting air passing through a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
A flat or scaphoid abdomen suggesting isolated esophageal atresia without a distal fistula

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the neck and listen to the cry
findings.finding: No stridor and a normal cry, arguing against isolated laryngeal or vocal cord pathology
Normal S1 and S2 without a new murmur, though a murmur may be present if there is an associated congenital heart defect

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perineum and confirm a patent anus
findings.finding: A normally positioned, patent anus, arguing against isolated anorectal malformation

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the limbs and spine
findings.finding: No limb reduction defects or obvious vertebral anomalies, though these may be part of a VACTERL association

labs.caveat: Leukocytosis is not expected from the atresia itself; it suggests aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia from secretions entering the airway.
Low bicarbonate from respiratory acidosis or metabolic derangement in a distressed newborn; not specific to esophageal atresia.
Hyponatremia can occur with SIADH or fluid shifts in a sick neonate; check before and after surgery.
Hypoglycemia is common in premature or growth-restricted newborns who cannot feed; correct before surgery.
Elevated when aspiration has caused pneumonitis or pneumonia; a normal value does not exclude it early.

findings.finding: Normal sinus rhythm; no arrhythmia specific to esophageal atresia
Sinus tachycardia from respiratory distress, hypoxemia or pain
Right axis deviation is normal in a newborn; abnormal axis may reflect an associated congenital heart defect
Right bundle branch block or other conduction abnormality suggesting an associated cardiac anomaly

imaging.preferred_when: First-line study in any newborn with suspected esophageal atresia

findings.text: Coiled feeding tube in the upper esophageal pouch (the tube cannot be advanced past the obstruction)
Gasless abdomen suggesting isolated esophageal atresia without a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
Air in the stomach and bowel suggesting a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
Aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia in the right upper lobe
Vertebral or rib anomalies suggesting VACTERL association

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or a fistula without atresia is suspected

findings.text: Contrast passing from the trachea into the esophagus (tracheoesophageal fistula)

imaging.preferred_when: Before surgical repair to define cardiac anatomy

findings.text: Associated congenital heart defect (e.g., ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot)
Renal anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis or hydronephrosis

imaging.preferred_when: Screening for vertebral and spinal cord anomalies in VACTERL association

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis by showing a coiled feeding tube in the proximal esophageal pouch and defines distal gas
Baseline white count and hemoglobin before surgery; leukocytosis may suggest aspiration pneumonia
Assesses electrolytes, glucose and renal function in a newborn who cannot feed
Detects associated congenital heart disease that affects surgical planning and anesthesia
initial.only_if: before surgical repair or when a murmur or cyanosis is present

confirmatory.why: Defines the anatomy and identifies a tracheoesophageal fistula when the plain film is equivocal
confirmatory.only_if: diagnosis is uncertain or an isolated fistula is suspected

supporting.why: Screens for renal anomalies as part of VACTERL association
Screens for vertebral and spinal cord anomalies
supporting.only_if: vertebral anomalies are seen on x-ray or VACTERL is suspected

supporting.why: Supports aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia when respiratory symptoms are prominent

not_indicated.why: CT is not needed; plain films and contrast studies define the anatomy with less radiation
MRI is not a first-line test for esophageal atresia
Urinalysis does not help diagnose esophageal atresia
Pancreatic enzymes are not relevant to this congenital anomaly
No role in the evaluation of a newborn with feeding and respiratory symptoms

decision_points: Do not feed a newborn with suspected esophageal atresia; keep the infant NPO and suction secretions
Confirm the diagnosis with a feeding tube attempt and chest/abdominal x-ray before any oral contrast
Evaluate for VACTERL association (cardiac, renal, vertebral, anorectal, limb) before surgery
Stabilize airway, breathing and glucose before transfer to a pediatric surgical center

differential.name: Tracheoesophageal fistula without esophageal atresia
differential.why_considered: Both cause coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds in a newborn from a connection between the airway and esophagus
differential.trigger: Feeding-related choking and cyanosis with a feeding tube that passes normally into the stomach

history: Feeding tube passes easily into the stomach
Symptoms may be intermittent and appear with the first feeds rather than immediately after birth
Recurrent aspiration and respiratory infections
exam: Copious secretions are less prominent than in atresia
Cyanosis and coughing specifically during swallowing
labs: Leukocytosis or elevated CRP if aspiration pneumonia has developed
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a normally positioned feeding tube in the stomach
Contrast esophagogram demonstrates contrast passing from the esophagus into the trachea

differential.name: Choanal atresia
differential.why_considered: Newborn with respiratory distress, cyanosis and difficulty feeding from an obstructed upper airway
differential.trigger: Cyanosis that worsens when the infant is at rest and improves with crying

history: Cyanosis at rest that improves with crying
Unable to pass a nasal catheter through the nose
Feeding difficulty because the infant cannot breathe and feed through the nose
exam: Inability to pass a nasal catheter beyond a few centimeters
Feeding tube passes into the stomach without resistance
imaging: CT or nasal endoscopy confirms a bony or membranous obstruction of the posterior nasal choanae
Chest and abdominal x-ray shows a normal feeding tube position and no esophageal pouch

differential.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
differential.why_considered: Newborn with respiratory distress, cyanosis and feeding difficulty
differential.trigger: Severe respiratory distress with a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest

history: Respiratory distress immediately after birth, often severe
Symptoms are not specifically related to feeding
Prenatal ultrasound may have shown bowel in the chest
exam: Scaphoid abdomen with bowel sounds heard in the chest
Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
Feeding tube passes into the stomach
imaging: Chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the hemithorax with mediastinal shift
No coiled feeding tube in the upper esophagus

differential.name: Neonatal pneumonia or aspiration pneumonitis
differential.why_considered: Newborn with tachypnea, cyanosis, coughing and feeding difficulty

history: Respiratory symptoms may precede or occur independently of feeding
Feeding tube passes into the stomach
Risk factors such as prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever
exam: Crackles or decreased breath sounds on chest auscultation
No choking specifically with the first swallows
labs: Blood culture may grow an organism
imaging: Chest x-ray shows focal or diffuse infiltrates without a coiled feeding tube
Normal esophageal anatomy on contrast study if performed

differential.name: Laryngotracheal cleft
differential.why_considered: Newborn with coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds from an abnormal connection between the airway and esophagus

history: Feeding tube passes into the stomach
Hoarse or weak cry
Recurrent aspiration
imaging: Direct laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy show a cleft between the larynx or trachea and the esophagus
Contrast esophagogram may show spillover into the airway

differential.name: Esophageal stenosis or web
differential.why_considered: Feeding difficulty and vomiting in an infant from a narrowed esophagus

history: Feeding tube may pass with resistance or not at all
Symptoms may be milder and present later than in atresia
Vomiting of undigested food
imaging: Contrast esophagogram shows a narrowed segment or web without a blind-ending pouch
Chest x-ray may show a feeding tube coiled above the narrowing

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Infant with spitting up, coughing and choking with feeds

history: Symptoms typically begin after the first weeks of life, not immediately after birth
Feeding tube passes into the stomach
Vomiting is common after feeds but the infant can swallow
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a normal feeding tube position
Contrast study shows reflux without a blind-ending pouch or fistula

severity.mild: Newborn with copious oral secretions and feeding difficulty but no respiratory distress; feeding tube cannot be passed; stable vitals
severity.moderate: Newborn with coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds, mild respiratory distress, and possible aspiration; requires NPO and suctioning
severity.severe: Newborn with significant respiratory distress, hypoxemia, and aspiration pneumonitis; needs urgent airway management and transfer to a pediatric surgical center
severity.critical: Newborn with apnea, severe hypoxemia, or respiratory failure from aspiration; requires immediate intubation and intensive care

red_flags.finding: Inability to pass a feeding tube into the stomach
red_flags.meaning: Confirms esophageal obstruction and should prompt immediate chest and abdominal x-ray

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis or choking with the first feed
red_flags.meaning: Suggests aspiration and a tracheoesophageal connection; stop feeds immediately

red_flags.finding: Copious frothy oral secretions requiring frequent suctioning
red_flags.meaning: Classic for esophageal atresia; keep the infant NPO and suction

red_flags.finding: Respiratory distress with grunting, retractions or apnea
red_flags.meaning: Indicates severe aspiration or airway compromise; needs urgent airway management

red_flags.finding: Abdominal distension with air in the stomach
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a distal tracheoesophageal fistula; air passes from the trachea into the stomach

red_flags.finding: Scaphoid abdomen with no air in the stomach
red_flags.meaning: Suggests isolated esophageal atresia without a distal fistula

complications.name: Anastomotic leak after repair
clues: Chest tube drainage of saliva or gastric contents
Pneumothorax or pleural effusion on x-ray

complications.name: Anastomotic stricture
clues: Dysphagia or feeding difficulty after repair
Narrowing at the anastomosis on contrast study

complications.name: Recurrent tracheoesophageal fistula
clues: Return of coughing and choking with feeds after repair
Contrast study showing a recurrent connection

special_populations.differences: Premature or small-for-gestational-age infants may have milder or delayed symptoms; diagnosis may be suspected only when a feeding tube cannot be passed or respiratory distress develops.

Rarely, a mild or missed case presents later in childhood with recurrent aspiration, coughing with feeds, or failure to thrive; this is more typical of an isolated tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia.

key_questions.question: Did the baby have trouble with the very first feed — choking, coughing, gagging or turning blue?
key_questions.looking_for: Choking, gagging and cyanosis with the first swallows of milk, which is the classic presentation of esophageal atresia

key_questions.question: Is the baby drooling or spitting up a lot of frothy white secretions, more than a normal newborn?
key_questions.looking_for: Copious frothy oral secretions that keep pooling and need frequent suctioning

key_questions.question: When did these symptoms start — right after birth or later?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset within the first hours to days of life, often at the first feeding; later onset argues against atresia

key_questions.question: Has the baby been able to keep any feeds down, or does everything come back up?
key_questions.looking_for: Feeds are not tolerated and are regurgitated or coughed up; the infant cannot swallow normally

key_questions.question: Is the baby breathing fast, grunting, or working hard to breathe?
key_questions.looking_for: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting or cyanosis suggesting aspiration and respiratory compromise

key_questions.question: Does the baby's belly look swollen or bloated?
key_questions.looking_for: Distension suggests a distal tracheoesophageal fistula letting air into the stomach; a flat or scaphoid abdomen suggests isolated atresia

key_questions.question: Was there extra fluid around the baby during the pregnancy (polyhydramnios)?
key_questions.looking_for: Polyhydramnios, a strong risk factor because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid

key_questions.question: Was the baby born early or small for gestational age?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or low birth weight, which are common and can blunt or delay the classic symptoms

key_questions.question: Did the pregnancy or delivery have any complications, or did prenatal ultrasounds show anything abnormal?
key_questions.looking_for: Polyhydramnios, prenatal findings of a small or absent stomach bubble, or other anomalies suggesting VACTERL

key_questions.question: Has anyone tried to pass a feeding tube, and did it go into the stomach?
key_questions.looking_for: A tube that meets resistance and coils in the upper esophagus rather than reaching the stomach

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any fever, lethargy or episodes of stopping breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, lethargy or apnea suggesting aspiration pneumonitis, sepsis or respiratory failure

key_questions.question: Does the baby have any other known birth defects, such as heart, kidney, spine or anal problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Features of VACTERL association, which changes preoperative planning and prognosis

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of esophageal or tracheal problems, or of babies who could not feed?
key_questions.looking_for: Most cases are sporadic; a rare affected sibling or parent suggests a familial form

reasoning_points: A newborn with copious frothy oral secretions and choking, gagging and cyanosis with the first feed
Inability to pass a feeding tube into the stomach, with the tube coiling in the upper esophageal pouch
Chest and abdominal x-ray showing a coiled feeding tube in the proximal esophageal pouch
Distal gas on x-ray suggesting a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, or a gasless abdomen suggesting isolated atresia
Polyhydramnios during pregnancy as a supporting risk factor
Screening for VACTERL association (cardiac, renal, vertebral, anorectal, limb anomalies) before surgery
Keeping the infant NPO with suctioning of secretions to prevent aspiration
Excluding look-alikes such as isolated tracheoesophageal fistula, choanal atresia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia and neonatal pneumonia

easy: Full-term newborn with copious frothy secretions noted immediately after birth
Choking, gagging and cyanosis with the first feed
Feeding tube cannot be passed and coils in the upper esophagus
Chest x-ray shows the coiled tube in the proximal esophageal pouch
medium: Premature or small-for-gestational-age infant with milder or delayed symptoms
Diagnosis suspected only because a feeding tube will not pass
Abdominal distension from a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
Aspiration pneumonitis with crackles and leukocytosis obscuring the underlying anomaly
Associated congenital heart defect found on preoperative echocardiogram
hard: Isolated tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia: feeding tube passes normally and symptoms are intermittent
Infant presenting later in childhood with recurrent aspiration, coughing with feeds or failure to thrive
Scaphoid abdomen with no distal gas suggesting isolated atresia without a fistula
Coexisting VACTERL anomalies that dominate the initial presentation
Respiratory distress severe enough to mimic primary lung disease or congenital diaphragmatic hernia
